articles.title: HS2’s tunnel boring machines are halfway to Euston
articles.excerpt: The two machines digging HS2’s tunnels from Old Oak Common are now halfway to Euston, having drilled 2.25 miles of their 4.5-mile journey. The TBM being pushed up to the tunnel starting site in March
articles.imageAlt: HS2’s tunnel boring machines are halfway to Euston
articles.body:
The two machines digging HS2’s tunnels from Old Oak Common are now halfway to Euston, having drilled 2.25 miles of their 4.5-mile journey. The TBM being pushed up to the tunnel starting site in March 2026 (c) HS2 By 17th November, both machines were between West Hampstead and Kilburn High Road stations and are due to finish digging in 2027, stopping underground on the approach to Euston, where HS2’s central London terminus is planned. The machines, named Karen and Madeleine, launched from Old Oak Common in January and March 2026 respectively and work around the clock, advancing about 16 metres a day. As they dig, the machines install precast concrete segments to line the tunnels. The Euston tunnels will require total of 48,294 segments, which are being made in Hartlepool, and the tunnelling is expected to generate about 1.5 million tonnes of excavated material, which is sent back to Old Oak Common, then dispatched by rail for landscaping elsewhere. Inside the Euston tunnel (c) HS2 Once the machines stop, workers will dismantle the TBM and remove most of it back through the completed tunnels. The 8.53-metre-wide cutting heads will be left buried in the ground initially, but when the large Euston cavern is constructed next to the tunnel, it will release the cutting heads for disposal. However, the steel can shields at the front of the machines will be left in place and will form part of the HS2 railway tunnel. That means when HS2 trains arrive or leave Euston station, they will pass through a remaining part of the machine that dug the tunnels. HS2’s chief executive Mark Wild said: “Reaching the halfway mark for building the programme’s last deep bored tunnel is a magnificent achievement by everyone involved. Their work driving the high speed line into central London is fundamental to the long term ambition of increasing the prosperity of the area around Euston. I wish everyone a safe journey to their final destination.” Interactive route map (c) HS2 The tunnel drilling operation is run by HS2’s London tunnelling contractor, the Skanska Costain STRABAG joint venture.

Source: Ian Visits
articles.author: Old Oak Town

articles.title: Euston station’s disused Platform 17 gets a new job hauling HS2 spoil
articles.excerpt: Euston station is getting heavy-duty freight trains again, as a dedicated route has opened to carry spoil out of the HS2 construction site. Rail Minister and Leader of Camden Council waving off freigh
articles.imageAlt: Euston station’s disused Platform 17 gets a new job hauling HS2 spoil
articles.body:
Euston station is getting heavy-duty freight trains again, as a dedicated route has opened to carry spoil out of the HS2 construction site. Rail Minister and Leader of Camden Council waving off freight train at Euston (c) HS2 Now that it’s open, trains from Euston’s now-disused Platform 17 will remove up to 170,000 tonnes of excavated material by rail, including 35,000 tonnes already moved during trials. HS2 says the programme will avoid more than 10,000 lorry journeys on roads around Euston and across London. Rail Minister Lord Hendy and Camden Council’s new leader, Cllr James Slater, were at Euston station on Monday (16th November) to see off a freight train hauled by Green Progressor. The trains run to Forders Sidings in Bedfordshire, where the excavated material will be reused at the Stewartby Brickworks development. HS2’s construction partner, the Mace Dragados joint venture, has begun digging down around seven metres to the level where the new station’s platforms will be built. Around 135,000 tonnes of material are expected to leave Euston by rail over the next ten months. When needed, GB Railfreight will run up to two trains a day alongside Euston’s passenger services. Each will have two locomotives and up to 12 wagons, carrying around 715 tonnes, equivalent to about 45 lorry loads. Trials between February and September showed the trains could carry more material than originally expected and run reliably around the passenger timetable. Slater said Camden had been calling for construction material to be removed from Euston by rail for years. “Taking more than 10,000 lorries off Camden’s roads is a significant achievement that will reduce disruption for our residents and businesses, improve air quality and help cut carbon emissions.” HS2 has already used freight trains to deliver tunnel segments to West Ruislip and Willesden and to remove millions of tonnes of excavated material from construction sites around Old Oak Common. Track 17 is expected to remain available until early 2029, and HS2 is looking at whether the loading facility could also serve other construction work around Euston. You can track train movements on RealTimeTrains, but note that they show up in the timetable as reserved spaces, but that doesn’t always mean a train will run, as they run as needed. If you’re using RealTimeTrains, search for Euston station, go to Detailed, then in the TOC menu select ZZ and set the time to All Day. Then you’re looking for the MBR (Materials by Train) service, and that’s the HS2 spoil trains.

Source: Ian Visits

articles.title: The Elizabeth line’s newest rail inspector has four legs and a laser
articles.excerpt: If you spot a robot dog on the Elizabeth line, don’t worry, it’s just sniffing out problems on the line. (c) Createc The four-legged robot, named Spot, was built by Boston Dynamics and is taking part
articles.imageAlt: The Elizabeth line’s newest rail inspector has four legs and a laser
articles.body:
If you spot a robot dog on the Elizabeth line, don’t worry, it’s just sniffing out problems on the line. (c) Createc The four-legged robot, named Spot, was built by Boston Dynamics and is taking part in a trial led by TfL and Createc, a technology firm based in Cockermouth, Cumbria. Spot’s trick is to build a detailed digital map as it walks. A laser scanner measures the surfaces around it, giving engineers a record of the tunnel or platform. By comparing scans taken at different times, they could spot changes and work out where a closer inspection is needed. The trial will help establish whether this new breed of railway inspector can make surveys quicker and reduce the time staff need to spend in potentially hazardous areas on live railway tracks. View this post on Instagram A post shared by TfL (@transportforlondon) “Railway tunnels and stations are complex environments to inspect and maintain, and robotics offers some really interesting opportunities to support engineers in understanding the condition of their infrastructure whilst also looking to remove people from potential harm.” said Will Newsom, chief executive of Createc. Createc works with Boston Dynamics to fit robots with specialist sensors for use in industries including nuclear power and infrastructure. The Elizabeth line trial, which also involves scanning technology company Emesent, gives the team a chance to see how the kit performs on a working railway. TfL highlighted the project as part of National Engineering Day.

Source: Ian Visits

articles.title: Almost no Elizabeth line services running on the last weekend of the month
articles.excerpt: The Elizabeth line will be largely closed over the final weekend of November as Transport for London (TfL) warns passengers to seek alternative routes. The closure affects most of the line on Saturday
articles.imageAlt: Almost no Elizabeth line services running on the last weekend of the month
articles.body:
The Elizabeth line will be largely closed over the final weekend of November as Transport for London (TfL) warns passengers to seek alternative routes. The closure affects most of the line on Saturday 28th and Sunday 29th November. In fact, the only bit running will be a two trains an hour shuttle between Reading and Maidenhead, which some folk may remember wasn’t even going to be part of the Elizabeth line when it was first planned. The extension from Maidenhead to Reading was added later. Services in the east and central sections are closed to allow for rail and crossing renewals, and maintenance of overhead line equipment. Services in the west are closed because Network Rail is carrying out a major overhaul of Dolphin Junction near Slough, meaning no trains on any service can enter or leave Paddington. That also means no GWR or Heathrow Express services either. TfL rail replacement bus services will operate on affected sections of the Elizabeth line including: Stratford to Romford Shenfield to Chadwell Heath/Newbury Park Ealing Broadway to Slough Slough to Maidenhead For people heading to Heathrow Airport, the Heathrow Express from Paddington will not run, but the Piccadilly line to Heathrow will be running normally. Trish Ashton, TfL’s Director of Rail, said: “We understand that these closures can impact customers’ journeys and would like to thank them for their patience while this essential work takes place. The work we’re carrying out is essential to maintaining the safety and reliability of the Elizabeth line for the millions of customers who rely it on every year. “We encourage customers to plan ahead, allow extra time for their journeys and check before they travel on TfL’s Journey Planner or the TfL Go app. Rail replacement buses and alternative travel options will be available throughout the closure.” For rail nerds, the closure is also seeing some GWR trains from the west of England and Wales diverted to Euston station.

Source: Ian Visits

articles.title: HS2 development around Euston could support 6,000 new homes
articles.excerpt: More than 6,000 new homes could be built around Euston as part of the HS2 development, with proposals spanning railway land, housing estates, and redevelopment sites from Bloomsbury to Camley Street.
articles.imageAlt: HS2 development around Euston could support 6,000 new homes
articles.body:
More than 6,000 new homes could be built around Euston as part of the HS2 development, with proposals spanning railway land, housing estates, and redevelopment sites from Bloomsbury to Camley Street. Euston housing zones (c) MHCLG A high-level brochure produced by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) sets out, in broad terms, a 30-plus-year plan to build new housing and neighbourhoods around Euston station. The plan extends beyond the redevelopment of Euston station itself, identifying six surrounding zones where additional housing could be built. One of the earliest projects would be at Regent’s Park Estate North, where council-led proposals could deliver around 500 new homes. The brochure presents this as a starting point for wider investment and potential renewal across the estate. A substantial opportunity also lies at Euston station and its railway cuttings, with housing potentially built above and alongside the tracks, as well as on land associated with HS2. Sites identified include the former Royal Mail site, Maria Fidelis and Starcross Street. The brochure argues that these should be considered together to make the most of the available land, rather than developed as isolated plots. The report also suggests that reconfiguring railway infrastructure, consolidating servicing facilities, and improving access could free up more space for development, allowing new homes to be built in phases alongside the transport works. Across the existing Regent’s Park Estate, the proposals envisage a longer-term estate renewal programme and additional housing, developed with existing residents. Addressing overcrowding is one reason for exploring new homes in and around the estate. The nearby Barracks site is also mentioned as a possible development opportunity, although only if its operational requirements change. It is currently expected to remain in use. South of the station, Euston Road and Bloomsbury could accommodate housing through redevelopment along the main road and the potential conversion or replacement of some institutional buildings. Within Bloomsbury, the brochure suggests repurposing some educational or institutional buildings for housing where they are less suitable for their current use. This would depend on providing replacement educational space and respecting the area’s established character. To the east and north-east of the station, Somers Town and Mornington Crescent offer further opportunities through estate renewal. The sixth area is Camley Street, where a first phase of regeneration already has planning consent for a mixed-use neighbourhood containing new homes, affordable housing and employment space. The brochure calls for housing and neighbourhood renewal to become central objectives of the Euston programme. It also acknowledges that surrounding communities have endured prolonged disruption while seeing limited benefits so far. Although the report expects there to be a significant proportion of affordable and social rented housing, it does not set an overall percentage or outline any planning designs for the new estates. At this stage, it’s more about setting out very broad aspirations while leaving the dirty details to later. The next step is a Strategic Delivery Framework, due to be developed during 2026–27, which would examine infrastructure, funding, viability and the order in which sites could come forward. The proposed timetable also points towards establishing a Locally Led Urban Development Corporation for Euston in 2027. If that deadline is met, then some of the new houses might even be built in time for Euston station’s bicentenary in 2037. The brochure is here.

Source: Ian Visits
articles.author: Old Oak Town

articles.title: No Elizabeth line between Stratford and Romford over Christmas
articles.excerpt: Major railway works in East London mean there will be no Elizabeth line services between Stratford and Romford over Christmas. Engineering works on Anglia route (c) Network Rail The closure is due to
articles.imageAlt: No Elizabeth line between Stratford and Romford over Christmas
articles.body:
Major railway works in East London mean there will be no Elizabeth line services between Stratford and Romford over Christmas. Engineering works on Anglia route (c) Network Rail The closure is due to major engineering work on the Great Eastern Main Line at Forest Gate, where Network Rail plans a 10-day programme to renew six sets of points, along with associated rails, sleepers and ballast. The Great Eastern Main Line at Forest Gate is a critical artery into the capital, supporting hundreds of passenger services every day and enabling freight trains to transport goods and supplies across the country as part of the strategic freight network. However, the track renewal will affect Greater Anglia and Elizabeth line services on the Great Eastern Main Line to and from London Liverpool Street. Martin Beable, Chief Operating Officer for GBR Anglia said: “While most of the railway will remain open as usual over the festive period, we’ll be taking advantage of a quieter time on the network to carry out significant improvements at Forest Gate and Barking station. “We’re also carrying out lots of smaller projects across East Anglia on Christmas Day and Boxing Day which will help us maintain a safe, reliable and efficient railway for the hundreds of passenger and freight services that use these routes every day. “We’re grateful for passengers’ patience while this work takes place and would encourage anyone travelling over Christmas and New Year to check their journey before setting off.” Unrelated works west of London will also mean no Elizabeth line west of Paddington – leaving just a shuttle service in the centre running. Travel Information: Friday 25 and Saturday 26 December 2026 – all routes As usual, trains will not run on most routes on Christmas Day and Boxing Day. A limited Stansted Express service will operate on Boxing Day between Stansted Airport and Tottenham Hale only. Trains will call at Tottenham Hale, Cheshunt, Harlow Town, Bishops Stortford and Stansted Airport. Cheshunt station will be open between approximately 10:30-19:45 Sunday 27th December 2026 to 3rd January 2027 During the 10 days of engineering work at Forest Gate, a rail replacement service will operate between Ingatestone/Shenfield and Newbury Park (London Underground station). Greater Anglia customers’ tickets will be accepted between Newbury Park and Stratford / Liverpool Street. Elizabeth line trains will not operate between Stratford and Romford, and a rail replacement bus service will operate. A reduced train service will run between Romford and Shenfield. Note: the Liberty Line will operate, so you may be able to get from Romford to Upminster and continue your journey that way as well. Slower, but no buses involved.

Source: Ian Visits
